standard_text: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths using unit cubes of the appropriate unit fraction edge lengths (e.g., using technology or concrete materials) and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths of the prism. Apply the formulas V = lwh and V = Bh to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths to solve real-world and other mathematical problems.

progression.narrative: 6.GM.4 asks students to find the volume of a right rectangular prism when one or more edges are fractions, first by packing it with unit-fraction cubes and showing the count matches the edge product, then by applying V = l x w x h and V = B x h to real and mathematical problems. The on-grade skills build in that order: extend the formula to a single fractional edge, prove that eight half-inch cubes make one cubic inch so cube count and volume separate, scale up to two and three fractional edges, apply the formulas in context, and read B as a finished base area. Students who struggle here almost always carry gaps from earlier grades. The most common are shaky fraction multiplication and a thin picture of volume as layers of unit cubes, both grade 5 work, sitting on top of even older gaps in whole-number multiplication and rectangle area. Intervention should rebuild those layers from the bottom, then return to the fractional edges.

steps.rationale: Extend V = lwh to one fractional edge. The layer picture from grade 5 still works -- a 1/2-unit height is half a layer -- so this is the gentlest entry into the standard's 'fractional edge lengths' demand, and the first place the add-the-edges habit must be broken.

The standard's own words: pack with unit-fraction cubes AND show the result equals multiplying the edges. The insight that 8 half-inch cubes make one cubic inch is what separates cube COUNT from VOLUME -- everything after leans on it.

Full computational demand: V = lwh with two or three fractional or mixed-number dimensions -- the spec's medium and difficult tiers. Three messy factors is where the third dimension silently drops, so this step trains the three-factor habit.

The standard says 'to solve real-world and other mathematical problems.' Packing dice, filling sandboxes -- volume and cube-packing now do work inside a story, and answers must be counts or cubic units as the question demands.
The second named formula, V = Bh. Students must read B as a finished AREA -- l x w folded into one number -- which prepares them for prisms with non-rectangular bases in grade 7.

The spec's Above tier reverses the formula: given the volume, recover a missing edge or propose possible dimensions. Undoing multiplication with division is the bridge from this standard to equation solving and 7.GM.3.

skills.name: Multiply whole numbers fluently

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply two whole numbers using equal groups or an array.

skills.i_do_script: Multiplying is a fast way to count equal groups, and every volume problem later ends in it. Watch 6 x 4: I make 6 rows with 4 in each row and count 24, so 6 x 4 = 24. I never add the two numbers, because 6 + 4 is only 10 and that leaves most of the group uncounted. Say the groups out loud: 6 groups of 4 is 24.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the two factors instead of multiplying them
canonical_error.why: The student reads x as +. Multiplication means equal groups: 6 x 4 is 6 groups of 4, which is 24. Adding 6 and 4 gives 10 and leaves most of the group uncounted.

skills.item_template: A single whole-number multiplication with one-digit or small factors. Student gives the product. Short response fluency bank, no calculator.

redirect_script.stop: Did you add those numbers or multiply them?
redirect_script.prompt: Multiplication counts equal groups. For 6 x 4, make 6 rows of 4 and count, or add 4 six times. Adding 6 and 4 only gives 10 and misses the rest of the group.
redirect_script.praise: You counted the groups and multiplied, that is exactly it.

vocabulary.definition: A number being multiplied. In 6 x 4, both 6 and 4 are factors.
The answer to a multiplication. The product of 6 and 4 is 24.
Objects arranged in equal rows and columns, a picture of multiplication.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 multiplication with arrays and equal groups before returning to this skill.

worked_example_script.text: Draw 6 rows of dots with 4 dots in each row.
How many dots are in one row? How many rows are there?
This array shows 6 groups of 4. Counting all the dots gives 24, so 6 x 4 = 24. Multiplying is faster than adding 4 six times.
If a student says 10, they added 6 + 4. Point at the array: adding names just two numbers, but the array holds 24 dots.
Your turn: build 7 rows of 3 and tell me 7 x 3.

skills.name: Find the area of a rectangle by multiplying side lengths

prerequisite_skill.description: Find the area of a rectangle by covering it with unit squares and multiplying the side lengths.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A rectangle is 4 units long and 3 units wide. What is its area?

skills.i_do_script: Area tells how many unit squares cover a rectangle, and it is the picture underneath every base and layer in volume. Watch a 4 by 3 rectangle: one row holds 4 squares and there are 3 rows, so I multiply 4 x 3 = 12 square units. I do not add the sides, because 4 + 3 = 7 counts steps along an edge, not the squares inside. Multiply the two side lengths and label the answer in square units.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the two side lengths instead of multiplying them
canonical_error.example: For a 4 by 3 rectangle, writes 7 (4 + 3) instead of 12
canonical_error.why: The student combines the sides the way perimeter does. Area counts the squares inside, which is 3 rows of 4, so the side lengths must be multiplied, not added.

skills.item_template: A rectangle with whole-number side lengths, given in words or on a grid. Student multiplies the side lengths to find the area in square units. Short response fluency bank, no calculator.

sample_items.stem: A rectangle is 4 units long and 3 units wide. What is its area in square units?
A rectangle is 5 units by 2 units. What is its area in square units?
A rectangle is 6 units by 4 units. What is its area?
A rectangle is 7 units by 3 units. What is its area?
A square is 5 units on each side. What is its area?
A rectangle is 8 units by 2 units. What is its area?
A rectangle is 9 units by 2 units. What is its area?
One row of a rectangle holds 6 unit squares, and there are 3 rows. What is the area?

redirect_script.stop: Are you adding the sides or multiplying them?
redirect_script.prompt: Area counts the unit squares inside. Multiply the two side lengths: a 4 by 3 rectangle has 3 rows of 4 squares, so 12. Adding the sides counts an edge, not the inside.
redirect_script.praise: You multiplied the side lengths and labeled square units, that is area.

vocabulary.definition: The number of unit squares that cover a flat shape, labeled in square units.
A square that is 1 unit on every side, used to measure area.
How long one side of a rectangle is.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 area by tiling a rectangle with unit squares before returning to this skill.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a rectangle 4 squares wide and 3 squares tall on grid paper.
How many unit squares are in one row? How many rows fill the rectangle?
Each row has 4 squares and there are 3 rows, so the rectangle holds 4 x 3 = 12 unit squares. The area is 12 square units. Area multiplies the two side lengths.
If a student says 7, they added 4 + 3. That counts steps along part of the border, not the squares inside. Have them shade the squares and count 12.
Your turn: a rectangle is 5 wide and 2 tall. Shade it and give the area.

skills.name: Multiply fractions, whole numbers, and mixed numbers

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply a fraction by a fraction and a fraction by a whole number.

skills.i_do_script: Every fractional edge in a volume problem gets multiplied, so this move has to be automatic. Watch 2/3 x 1/2: I multiply the tops, 2 x 1 = 2, and the bottoms, 3 x 2 = 6, to get 2/6, which is 1/3. For a mixed number like 2 1/2 x 1 1/2, I first rewrite each as an improper fraction, 5/2 and 3/2, then multiply straight across to get 15/4, and rename it 3 3/4. I never multiply the whole parts and fraction parts separately, because that drops the cross pieces.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the whole parts and the fraction parts of a mixed number separately
canonical_error.example: For 2 1/2 x 1 1/2, computes 2 x 1 = 2 and 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4, then answers 2 1/4 instead of 3 3/4
canonical_error.why: The student treats a mixed number as two separate numbers. Multiplying has to cover both parts of both numbers, so splitting them drops the cross products 2 x 1/2 and 1 x 1/2. Rewriting as improper fractions keeps every piece.

skills.item_template: One multiplication: fraction by fraction, fraction by whole number, or mixed number by fraction or whole number. Numeric response, clean numbers, no calculator.

redirect_script.stop: Can a mixed number be split into two multiplications like that?
redirect_script.prompt: Rewrite each mixed number as an improper fraction first, then multiply straight across: top times top, bottom times bottom. 2 1/2 is 5/2 and 1 1/2 is 3/2.
redirect_script.praise: You converted to improper fractions and multiplied straight across, that method never misses a piece.

vocabulary.definition: The top number of a fraction, how many parts you have.
The bottom number of a fraction, how many equal parts make one whole.
A fraction whose top is bigger than its bottom, like 5/2, another way to write 2 1/2.
A whole number and a fraction together, like 2 1/2.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a square and cut it into 3 equal columns; shade 2 of them to show 2/3.
Now cut the same square into 2 rows and keep just 1 row. What part of the shaded 2/3 are we keeping?
Cutting the 2/3 into 2 equal rows and keeping one row leaves 2 out of 6 small rectangles, so 2/3 x 1/2 = 2/6 = 1/3. Multiplying tops and bottoms, 2 x 1 over 3 x 2, gives the same 2/6.
If a student answers 2/5 by adding, point at the grid: the small rectangles come from 3 x 2, not 3 + 2.
Your turn: multiply 3/4 x 1/2 by multiplying the tops and the bottoms.

practice_problems.stem: Maya wrote 2 1/2 x 1 1/2 = 2 1/4. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: She multiplied the whole parts and the fraction parts separately, which drops the cross pieces. Rewrite as improper fractions: 5/2 x 3/2 = 15/4 = 3 3/4.

activities.title: Part of a Part
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair gets a product like 2/3 x 1/2.
2. Shade 2/3 of a grid square in the first color by cutting it into 3 columns.
3. Cut the same square into 2 rows and outline just 1 row in the second color.
4. Count the small rectangles shaded in both: 2 out of 6, so 2/6 = 1/3.
5. Write 2/3 x 1/2 = 2/6 and check it against multiplying tops and bottoms. Repeat with 3/4 x 1/2 and 1/2 x 1/2.

activities.title: Improper First
materials: Card deck: mixed-number products and their improper-fraction setups
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each mixed-number product like 2 1/2 x 1 1/2 to its improper-fraction setup 5/2 x 3/2.
3. To claim a match, say the product as a mixed number out loud.
4. Two decoy cards used the split-the-parts error; set them aside and explain the mistake.

strategy_links.why: The area-model grid shows fraction multiplication as a part of a part before the top-times-top rule is named.
The split-the-mixed-number error is stable and predictable; finding and fixing it in worked examples confronts it directly.

questioning_prompts: Are these two numbers being multiplied or added? How can you tell?
What does 2/3 x 1/2 mean in the grid picture, a part of a part?
Why do we rewrite a mixed number as an improper fraction before multiplying?
When you multiply straight across, what happens to the tops? To the bottoms?
Is your product bigger or smaller than you started with, and does that make sense?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies the whole parts and fraction parts of a mixed number separately.
misconception_redirects.say: A mixed number is one quantity. Rewrite 2 1/2 as 5/2 and 1 1/2 as 3/2, then multiply straight across so no piece is dropped.
misconception_redirects.praise: You converted first, so every cross piece was counted.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds numerators and denominators instead of multiplying.
misconception_redirects.say: Multiplying is not adding. For 2/3 x 1/2, multiply the tops, 2 x 1, and the bottoms, 3 x 2, to get 2/6.
misconception_redirects.praise: You multiplied tops and bottoms, that is the rule.

quick_checks.look_for: 1/6, from 1 x 1 over 2 x 3, not 2/5 from adding.
5, from 5/2 x 2 = 10/2, not 4 1/2 from doubling only the whole part.

steps.annotation: Rewrite each mixed number as an improper fraction.
Set up the multiplication with the improper fractions.
Multiply straight across: 5 x 3 over 2 x 2.
Rename the improper fraction: 15/4 is 3 wholes and 3/4.
Rewrite each mixed number as an improper fraction.
Set up the multiplication.
Multiply straight across, top times top and bottom times bottom.
Rename the improper fraction as a mixed number.

sentence_starters: I rewrote ___ as ___ and ___ as ___ so I could multiply straight across.
The product is ___ because I multiplied the tops and the bottoms.

skills.name: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number edges

prerequisite_skill.description: Find volume by counting unit cubes and by multiplying the edge lengths of a prism with whole-number edges.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A box is 4 units by 3 units by 2 units. What is its volume?

skills.i_do_script: Volume counts the unit cubes that fill a box with no gaps, and the layer picture makes the formula obvious. Watch a 4 by 3 by 2 box: the bottom layer is 4 rows of 3, so 12 cubes, and 2 layers stack up, so 12 x 2 = 24 cubic units. That is exactly V = l x w x h, 4 x 3 x 2 = 24, and it is also V = B x h, where the base area B is 12. I never add the three edges, because 4 + 3 + 2 = 9 counts a path along the box, not the space inside.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the three edge lengths instead of multiplying them
canonical_error.example: For a 4 by 3 by 2 box, answers 9 (4 + 3 + 2) instead of 24
canonical_error.why: Three labeled numbers trigger the habit of adding. Volume is layers of cubes: 4 x 3 = 12 in one layer, taken 2 times, so the edges must be multiplied.

skills.item_template: A right rectangular prism with whole-number edges, given in words or as a base area with a height. Student finds the volume in cubic units. Numeric response, no calculator.

sample_items.stem: A box is 4 units by 3 units by 2 units. How many unit cubes fill it?
A box is 5 units by 2 units by 3 units. What is its volume in cubic units?
One layer of a box holds 12 cubes and the box holds 3 layers. What is the volume in cubic units?
A prism is 6 units by 2 units by 2 units. What is its volume in cubic units?
A cube is 3 units on each edge. What is its volume in cubic units?
A prism has a base area of 10 square units and a height of 4 units. What is the volume?
A box holds 18 unit cubes, each 1 cubic centimeter. What is the volume in cubic centimeters?
A prism is 7 units by 2 units by 1 unit. What is its volume in cubic units?

redirect_script.stop: Did you add those three edges or multiply them?
redirect_script.prompt: Volume multiplies. Count one layer first: length times width. Then multiply by the height to stack the layers. For 4 by 3 by 2, that is 12 then 24.
redirect_script.praise: You counted a layer and stacked it, that is volume.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of space inside a solid, counted in unit cubes.
A cube that is 1 unit on every edge, worth 1 cubic unit.
One flat level of unit cubes; a prism is layers stacked to its height.
The number of unit squares covering the bottom of a prism, equal to length times width.

worked_example_script.text: Build or sketch a box 4 cubes long, 3 cubes wide, and 2 cubes tall.
How many cubes are in just the bottom layer? What did you multiply to get it?
How many of those layers stack to the top?
One layer is 4 x 3 = 12 cubes, and 2 layers make 12 x 2 = 24 cubic units. That is V = l x w x h and also V = B x h with B = 12.
If a student says 9, they added 4 + 3 + 2. Have them build the bottom layer alone; seeing 12 cubes in one layer collapses the adding answer.
Your turn: how many unit cubes fill a 5 by 2 by 3 box? Talk through the layers.

practice_problems.stem: A box is 3 units by 2 units by 4 units. What is its volume in cubic units?
A box is 5 units by 2 units by 2 units. What is its volume in cubic units?
A prism is 6 units by 4 units by 2 units. What is its volume in cubic units?
A cube is 4 units on each edge. What is its volume in cubic units?
One layer of a box holds 10 unit cubes and the box has 4 layers. What is the volume in cubic units?
A prism has a base area of 12 square units and a height of 5 units. Use V = B x h to find the volume.
A prism is 7 units by 2 units by 2 units. What is its volume, and how does it compare to a 7 by 2 by 1 prism?
practice_problems.answer: 28 cubic units, which is double the 14 cubic units of the 7 by 2 by 1 prism because it has twice as many layers.

practice_problems.stem: Sam found the volume of a 4 by 3 by 2 box. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 24 cubic units. Volume multiplies the edges: V = 4 x 3 x 2 = 24. Adding the edges counts a path, not the cubes inside.

activities.title: Build and Count the Layers
activities.instructions:
1. Each group builds the bottom layer of a 4 by 3 box and counts it, 12 cubes.
2. Stack a second identical layer and count the total, 24.
3. Write V = 4 x 3 x 2 = 24 and circle the 12 as the base area B.
4. Rebuild as a 5 by 2 box with 3 layers and write V = 5 x 2 x 3 = 30.
5. Debrief: why does the height tell how many layers, and why do we multiply instead of add?

activities.title: Prism to Volume Match
activities.instructions:
1. Lay the dimension cards face up and the volume cards in a face-down pool.
2. Flip a volume card and race to match it to the prism whose edges produce it.
3. Defend every match out loud with V = l x w x h.
4. Two decoy volume cards are sums of the edges; if a pair grabs one, have them multiply to check.

strategy_links.why: Building layers with linking cubes grounds volume as stacked area before the formula is named.
The add-the-edges error is concrete and visible; find-and-fix work makes students say why volume multiplies.

questioning_prompts: Before you compute, are you adding or multiplying, and why does volume need multiplying?
How many cubes are in one layer of this prism?
What does the height tell you about the number of layers?
Where is the base area B in your prism, and what is it here?
Your answer is in cubic units. What did the word cubic tell us we counted?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds the three edges, such as 4 + 3 + 2 = 9.
misconception_redirects.say: Volume is layers of cubes, never a sum. Count one layer, 4 x 3 = 12, then multiply by 2 layers for 24.
misconception_redirects.praise: You counted a layer and stacked it, so the edges got multiplied.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies length and width but forgets the height.
misconception_redirects.say: You found one layer. The box is more than one layer tall, so multiply by the height to stack them.
misconception_redirects.praise: You added the height back in by multiplying, so all three edges counted.

quick_checks.prompt: A 5 by 2 by 3 box, volume in cubic units.
quick_checks.look_for: 30, from 5 x 2 x 3. A 10 means the student added the edges.

quick_checks.prompt: Base area 8 square units, height 4 units, volume?
quick_checks.look_for: 32, using V = B x h, not 12 from adding.

worked_solution.stem: Find the volume of a box that is 4 units by 3 units by 2 units.

steps.math: V = l x w x h
steps.annotation: Volume multiplies all three edges, never adds them.
Copy each edge into the formula.
Multiply length and width to count one layer: 4 x 3 = 12 cubes.
Multiply by the height to stack 2 layers: 12 x 2 = 24.

faded_example.stem: Find the volume of a box that is 5 units by 3 units by 2 units.

steps.math: V = l x w x h
steps.annotation: Volume multiplies all three edges.
Copy each edge into the formula.
Multiply length and width to count one layer.
Multiply by the height and label in cubic units.

sentence_starters: One layer holds ___ cubes, and there are ___ layers, so the volume is ___.
I multiplied ___ x ___ x ___ because volume counts cubes, not a path around the box.

skills.name: Calculate the volume of a prism with one fractional edge
skills.i_do_script: We're using V = l x w x h on a prism where one edge is a fraction. Model with a box 6 in. by 4 in. by 1/2 in.: the base layer is 6 x 4 = 24, and the height 1/2 means only half of that layer's worth of space, so 24 x 1/2 = 12 cubic inches. Point at each labeled edge on the figure as you use it -- students must see that all THREE numbers get multiplied, never added.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the three edge lengths instead of multiplying them
canonical_error.example: For a prism 6 in. x 4 in. x 1/2 in., student answers 10 1/2 (6 + 4 + 1/2) instead of 12 cubic inches
canonical_error.why: Three labeled numbers on a figure trigger the perimeter habit of combining by adding. The student hasn't anchored volume to the layer picture -- a 6 x 4 layer of cubes taken 1/2 time -- so the formula's multiplication feels arbitrary and addition sneaks in.

redirect_script.stop: Stop -- did you add those edges or multiply them?
redirect_script.prompt: Volume is multiplying, never adding. Write the formula V = l x w x h first, then copy one labeled number under each letter. Multiply the two whole numbers first, then multiply by the fraction.
redirect_script.praise: You wrote the formula, matched every edge to a letter, and multiplied all three. That's the whole skill.

skills.item_template: A labeled prism figure with two whole-number edges and one fractional or mixed-number edge. Student applies V = l x w x h. NR (numeric response), spec Below Proficiency shape.

sample_items.stem:
A rectangular prism is shown below.

What is the volume, in cubic inches, of the rectangular prism?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 10 1/2 (adding the three edges instead of multiplying) or 24 (multiplying only length and width)

sample_items.stem:
A rectangular prism is shown below.

What is the volume, in cubic centimeters, of the rectangular prism?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 10 1/2 (adding the three edges instead of multiplying) or 15 (multiplying only length and width)

sample_items.stem:
A rectangular prism is shown below.

What is the volume, in cubic feet, of the rectangular prism?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 10 3/4 (adding the three edges instead of multiplying) or 16 (multiplying only length and width)

sample_items.stem:
A rectangular prism is shown below.

What is the volume, in cubic inches, of the rectangular prism?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 12 1/2 (adding the three edges instead of multiplying) or 28 (multiplying only length and width)

vocabulary.definition: A box shape with 6 rectangular faces, like a cereal box.
The three measurements of a prism: length, width, and height.
The space inside a solid, found by l x w x h and labeled in cubic units.
A rule written with letters, like V = l x w x h, that works for any prism.

worked_example_script.text: Display a prism figure labeled l = 6 in., w = 4 in., h = 1/2 in.
What are the three dimensions of this prism? Point to each one on the figure.
What formula finds the volume of a rectangular prism?
Write V = l x w x h, then directly underneath: V = 6 x 4 x 1/2.
Which two numbers would you multiply first to keep it easy? What is 6 x 4?
Now 24 x 1/2 -- taking half of 24. What do you get?

If a student says 10 1/2, they added 6 + 4 + 1/2. Ask: 'Does adding the edges count any cubes inside the box?' Then rebuild the layer picture: 24 cubes in a full layer, but the box is only 1/2 unit tall.

V = 12 cubic inches. Notice the label -- CUBIC inches, because we're counting cube-sized chunks of space, and notice multiplying by 1/2 made the answer smaller than the base layer. That's normal with fractions.

practice_problems.stem: A prism is 3 in. long, 2 in. wide, and 4 in. tall. What is its volume in cubic inches?
A prism is 10 cm long, 2 cm wide, and 1/2 cm tall. What is its volume in cubic centimeters?
A rectangular prism is shown below. What is its volume in cubic inches?
practice_problems.notes: Watch for 11 1/2 -- the added-edges trap.

practice_problems.stem: A tile box measures 4 ft by 4 ft by 3/4 ft. How many cubic feet of space are inside?
Ava found the volume of a prism that is 8 in. long, 3 in. wide, and 1/2 in. tall. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 12 cubic inches. Volume multiplies the edges: V = 8 x 3 x 1/2 = 12. Adding the edges doesn't count any of the space inside the box.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical added-the-edges error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: A rectangular prism is shown below. What is its volume in cubic centimeters?
A prism has a volume of 10 cubic feet. Its length is 5 ft and its width is 4 ft. What is its height, in feet?
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- previews 6GM4-S6.

practice_problems.stem: Jon multiplied 5 x 2 x 1/2 to find a volume and got 5 cubic inches -- smaller than the 10 he got from 5 x 2 alone. Explain why multiplying by 1/2 made the volume smaller, using the layer picture.
practice_problems.answer: The base layer would hold 10 cubic inches if the prism were 1 inch tall, but the prism is only 1/2 inch tall -- half a layer. Half of 10 is 5, so multiplying by a fraction less than 1 shrinks the product.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why stretch; fights the 'multiplication always makes bigger' belief.

activities.title: Half-Layer Build
activities.instructions:
1. Groups build a 6-by-4 layer of cubes and count it (24).
2. Say: our prism is only HALF this tall. Ask groups to show what half a layer looks like (split the layer in two, keep one part).
3. Groups write the number sentence that matches what they built: 6 x 4 x 1/2 = 12.
4. Repeat with a 5-by-2 layer and a height of 1 1/2 (one full layer plus a half layer).
5. Debrief: why does the height tell us how many LAYERS, even when it's a fraction?

activities.title: Add or Multiply?
activities.instructions:
1. Show Marcus's work; pairs decide what he did with the three labeled edges.
2. Pairs write the correct formula V = l x w x h and recompute.
3. Debrief question: what does adding the edges measure -- anything at all? (Edge lengths laid end to end, not space.)

content.worked_problem: A prism is 7 in. long, 2 in. wide, and 1/2 in. tall. Marcus wrote: V = 7 + 2 + 1/2 = 9 1/2 cubic inches.
content.error_step: Marcus added the three edge lengths instead of multiplying them.
content.why: Volume counts the cubes inside: a 7 x 2 layer holds 14, and a 1/2-unit height means half a layer, so V = 7 x 2 x 1/2 = 7 cubic inches. Adding edges never counts space.

activities.title: Prism-to-Volume Match
materials: Card set (dimension cards and volume cards)
activities.instructions:
1. Deal the dimension cards face up and the volume cards face down in a pool.
2. Pairs flip a volume card and race to match it to the prism dimensions that produce it.
3. Every match must be defended out loud with V = l x w x h.
4. The decoys are sums of the edges -- if a pair grabs one, have them check by multiplying.

strategy_links.why: The added-the-edges error is concrete and visible -- find-and-fix work makes students articulate why volume multiplies.
Building half-layers with cubes grounds the fractional height before the formula goes abstract.
The formula routine (write V = lwh, match numbers, multiply) transfers cleanly through I-do / we-do / you-do.

questioning_prompts: Before you compute: are you adding or multiplying? How do you know volume needs multiplying?
Point to the figure -- which number is the length, the width, the height?
How many cubes are in one full layer of this prism? What does the height do to that layer?
Your answer is labeled cubic inches. What does the word 'cubic' tell us we counted?
Which two numbers did you multiply first, and why did you pick them?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds the three edge lengths -- e.g., writes 6 + 4 + 1/2 = 10 1/2 for a 6 x 4 x 1/2 prism.
misconception_redirects.say: Volume is multiplying, never adding. Write the formula V = l x w x h first, then copy one labeled number under each letter. Multiply the two whole numbers first, then multiply by the fraction.
misconception_redirects.praise: You wrote the formula, matched every edge to a letter, and multiplied all three. That's the whole skill.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student refuses to multiply by the fraction ('the answer got smaller, that can't be right') and rounds 1/2 up to 1.
misconception_redirects.say: A height of 1/2 inch means the box holds only HALF a layer of cubes. Smaller than a full layer is exactly right. Multiply by the fraction as written.
misconception_redirects.praise: You trusted the fraction -- a shorter box really does hold less.

quick_checks.prompt: Thumbs check: for a 5 x 2 x 1/2 prism, is the volume 7 1/2 or 5?
quick_checks.look_for: Instant 5. A 7 1/2 means the student added the edges -- rebuild the layer picture before moving on.

skills.name: Show that packing unit-fraction cubes matches multiplying the edges
skills.i_do_script: This is the 'show it two ways' skill: pack a prism with small cubes AND multiply the edges, and prove both give the same volume. worked_example_script.text: Display a prism labeled 2 in. long, 1 in. wide, 1 in. tall, packed with 1/2-inch cubes.

skills.name: Apply V = lwh when two or three edges are fractional
skills.i_do_script: Volume is stacked floors: the bottom of the box is one flat layer, and the height counts how many of those layers pile up -- so a two-factor answer only ever buys you the floor. canonical_error.why: Area problems trained a two-factor habit (l x w), and with fractions the working memory is full after one multiplication -- the third factor, often the fraction, silently drops. The student is computing a face's area, not the space inside.

This is the danger moment -- students write 10 and stop. If that happens, point at the figure: 'You have three checks to earn and only two so far. Which edge hasn't been used?'

A box 3 in. long, 1 1/2 in. wide, and 1 in. tall is filled with 1/2-inch dice. How many dice fill the box?

practice_problems.stem: A crate 2 1/2 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 1/2 ft tall is packed with boxes that are cubes with 1/2-ft sides. How many boxes fit?
A box 4 in. long, 1 in. wide, and 1/2 in. tall is filled with 1/2-inch cubes. Tran found how many cubes fit. Find his mistake and fix it.

practice_problems.answer: 16 cubes. Tran divided by the cube's EDGE (1/2 in.) instead of its VOLUME. One cube is 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8 cubic inch, so 2 / (1/8) = 16. Check by counting: 8 x 2 x 1 = 16.

practice_problems.stem: Can a box 2 in. x 2 in. x 1 in. be filled COMPLETELY (no gaps) with 3/4-inch cubes? Explain using division.
practice_problems.answer: No. Along a 2-inch edge, 2 / (3/4) = 2 2/3 -- not a whole number of cubes, so a gap is left. Complete packing needs every edge to be a whole-number multiple of the cube's edge.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why stretch about when packing works at all.

activities.title: Dice in a Box
activities.instructions:
1. Groups measure the box's inside dimensions to the nearest half inch.
2. Predict: how many dice will fill it? Write the prediction.
3. Pack one full ROW along the length and count; then one full layer; then estimate the layers.
4. Compute cubes-per-edge x cubes-per-edge x layers and compare to the prediction and to the actual packing.
5. Debrief: where did the calculation and the real box disagree, and why? (Leftover gaps when an edge isn't a multiple of the die.)

activities.title: Edge or Volume?
activities.instructions:
1. Show Nia's work; pairs decide what the 1/2 in her division actually was.
2. Pairs compute one cube's volume, redo the division, and verify by counting cubes along each edge.
3. Debrief question: what units was Nia's answer in? (Cubic inches divided by inches isn't a count of anything.)

content.worked_problem: A box 2 in. x 2 in. x 1 in. is filled with 1/2-inch cubes. Nia wrote: V = 4 cubic inches, so 4 / (1/2) = 8 cubes.
content.error_step: Nia divided the box's volume by the cube's edge length (1/2 in.) instead of the cube's volume.
content.why: One 1/2-inch cube fills 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8 cubic inch. The count is 4 / (1/8) = 32 -- which matches counting 4 x 4 x 2 cubes along the edges.

activities.title: Packing Contractor
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair is a packing company. Draw a job card: a box with fractional dimensions and a cube size (for example, a 2 x 1 1/2 x 1 ft crate and 1/2-ft boxes).
2. The pair must quote the job: how many cubes, shown TWO ways (edge counting and volume division).
3. Quotes where the two ways disagree get rejected -- find the error before submitting.
4. Three accepted quotes wins. Debrief: which way caught more of your own mistakes?

strategy_links.why: Physically packing dice before dividing volumes keeps the division meaning-full -- count first, formalize second.
The two-road solution (edge counting vs. volume division) is exactly what a think-aloud makes visible.
Contrasting a correct volume division with the divide-by-edge error trains the units check that saves this skill.

worked_solution.stem: A box 3 in. long, 2 in. wide, and 1 in. tall is filled with dice that have 1/2-inch sides. How many dice fill the box?

steps.annotation: Count how many dice fit along each dimension -- each inch holds two 1/2-inch dice.
Dice per row, rows per layer, layers -- multiply the three counts.

steps.math: Check: box V = 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 cubic inches; one die = (1/2)^3 = 1/8 cubic inch
steps.annotation: Second road: find both volumes. The die's volume is 1/8, NOT 1/2 -- cube the edge.
Volume divided by volume gives the count. Both roads agree: 48.

Multiply the three counts.

skills.name: Apply V = Bh using the area of the base
skills.i_do_script: V = Bh is the same volume idea folded in half: B is the AREA of the base (a whole layer, already multiplied), and h counts the layers. Model with a base of 4 cm by 3 cm and a height of 2 1/2 cm: B = 4 x 3 = 12 square cm, then V = 12 x 2 1/2 = 30 cubic cm. Then show the shortcut case: if the problem already SAYS the base area is 12, you skip straight to 12 x 2 1/2. The capital B is an area, never an edge.

canonical_error.pattern: Finds the base area B by adding the base's length and width instead of multiplying
canonical_error.example: Base 4 cm by 3 cm, height 2 1/2 cm: student writes B = 4 + 3 = 7 and V = 7 x 2 1/2 = 17 1/2 instead of B = 12 and V = 30
canonical_error.why: The phrase 'the base' pulls up perimeter-flavored thinking -- combining the two edges additively. The student hasn't locked in that B is an AREA: squares covering the bottom, which requires length x width.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- is B the distance around the base, or the squares covering it?
redirect_script.prompt: B is the AREA of the base: the number of unit squares covering the bottom. Draw the base as a rectangle, and find how many squares cover it -- length TIMES width. Then multiply by the height.
redirect_script.praise: You found B as an area -- squares covering the base -- and then stacked it with the height. That's V = Bh working perfectly.

skills.item_template: Either the base area B is given directly with a (often fractional) height, or the base's length and width are given and the student finds B first. Apply V = Bh. NR (numeric response).

vocabulary.definition: The face a prism sits on -- for V = Bh it's the bottom rectangle.
The area of the base face, in SQUARE units; the capital B in V = Bh.
How tall the prism is -- the distance from base to top.
Areas are labeled in square units; volumes are labeled in cubic units.

worked_example_script.text: Display a prism with its base labeled 4 cm by 3 cm and its height labeled 2 1/2 cm. Write both formulas side by side: V = l x w x h and V = B x h.
These two formulas give the same volume. Looking at them, what do you think the capital B stands for?
The base is 4 cm by 3 cm. How many unit SQUARES cover that base? Is that adding or multiplying?
Write B = 4 x 3 = 12 sq cm. Shade the base on the figure.
If a student says B = 7, they added 4 + 3. Sketch the base as a 4-by-3 grid and count the squares -- 12, not 7. Adding gives you edge lengths laid end to end, not covering.
Now V = B x h = 12 x 2 1/2. What does multiplying by 2 1/2 mean in the layer picture?
What is 12 x 2 1/2? (Twelve, twice, plus half of twelve.)
V = 30 cubic cm. And here's the shortcut: if a problem hands you 'the base area is 12 sq cm,' the multiplying is already done -- go straight to 12 x 2 1/2. B is always an area, never an edge.

practice_problems.stem: The base of a prism has an area of 10 sq cm. The prism is 2 cm tall. Use V = Bh to find the volume in cubic centimeters.
A prism's base is 3 cm long and 2 cm wide. What is B, the area of the base, in square centimeters?
The base of a rectangular prism has an area of 14 sq in. The prism is 1 1/2 in. tall. What is its volume in cubic inches?
A prism's base is 4 1/2 cm by 2 cm, and its height is 3 cm. Find B, then use V = Bh to find the volume.
practice_problems.answer: B = 9 sq cm; V = 27 cubic centimeters

practice_problems.stem: A prism's base is 5 in. by 4 in., and its height is 1 1/2 in. Kira used V = Bh. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 30 cubic inches. B is the AREA of the base -- multiply, don't add: B = 5 x 4 = 20 sq in., then V = 20 x 1 1/2 = 30.
practice_problems.notes: The added-base-edges error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: The base of a prism has an area of 7 1/2 sq ft. The prism is 2 ft tall. What is its volume in cubic feet?
Prism A has base area 10 sq in. and height 3 in. Prism B has base area 15 sq in. and height 2 in. Which has the greater volume? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: Neither -- they're equal. A: 10 x 3 = 30 cubic inches; B: 15 x 2 = 30 cubic inches. A wider base with a shorter height can hold exactly the same space.
practice_problems.notes: Compare-and-explain stretch.

practice_problems.stem: A prism has a volume of 9 cubic cm and a height of 1 1/2 cm. Use V = Bh to find the area of its base, in square centimeters.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- previews 6GM4-S6.

activities.title: Two Formulas, One Volume
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out three columns of cards: prism dimensions, a V = Bh setup, and a volume.
2. Pairs build complete matches: dimensions -> the matching B and h -> the volume.
3. Every match must be read aloud as 'B is ___ BECAUSE ___ times ___.'
4. Debrief: what is B, and what units does it wear?

Base 5 in. x 2 in., height 1 1/2 in.

activities.title: What Is B, Really?
activities.instructions:
1. Show Sam's work; pairs decide what his '10' measures.
2. Pairs draw the 6-by-4 base on grid paper and COUNT the squares covering it.
3. Redo the volume with the counted B.
4. Debrief question: what does 6 + 4 measure on the drawing? (Two edges laid end to end -- not covering.)

content.worked_problem: A prism's base is 6 cm by 4 cm and its height is 1/2 cm. Sam wrote: B = 6 + 4 = 10, so V = 10 x 1/2 = 5 cubic centimeters.
content.error_step: Sam added the base's length and width to get B instead of multiplying.
content.why: B is the AREA of the base -- the unit squares covering it: 6 x 4 = 24 sq cm. So V = 24 x 1/2 = 12 cubic centimeters.

activities.title: Stack the Base
materials: A stack of identical rectangles (index cards work)
activities.instructions:
1. Groups cut a 4-by-3 base from grid paper and count its squares (B = 12).
2. Stack index cards on the base: each card is one 'layer' of the prism.
3. Ask: if each card were 1 cm thick and we stacked 2 1/2 cards' worth, how much space is that? (12 x 2 1/2.)
4. Debrief: V = Bh means 'a base's worth of cubes, h times.' What changes if the height is a fraction?

strategy_links.why: 'What is B, and why isn't it 7?' is a perfect turn-and-talk -- students must verbalize area vs. added edges.
The B = l + w error hides inside otherwise-correct work; find-and-fix keeps students inspecting the B line.
The two-step routine (find B, then multiply by h) hands off cleanly from modeling to guided to independent work.

questioning_prompts: What does the capital B stand for -- an edge, a distance around, or an area?
What units does B wear? What units does the volume wear?
The problem already gave you the base area. What multiplication is already done for you?
Where is the base on this figure? Shade it before you compute.
How is V = Bh the same as V = l x w x h? Where did l x w go?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student computes B by adding the base's length and width -- e.g., B = 4 + 3 = 7 for a 4 cm by 3 cm base.
misconception_redirects.say: B is the AREA of the base: the number of unit squares covering the bottom. Draw the base as a rectangle, and find how many squares cover it -- length TIMES width. Then multiply by the height.
misconception_redirects.praise: You found B as an area -- squares covering the base -- and then stacked it with the height. That's V = Bh working perfectly.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student is given B directly (say, 12 sq in.) but stalls hunting for a length and width, or multiplies B by both a made-up l and w.
misconception_redirects.say: The problem already did l x w for you -- that's what 12 square inches IS. One multiplication left: B times the height.
misconception_redirects.praise: You recognized B as a finished area and went straight to B x h. Efficient and correct.

quick_checks.prompt: A base is 5 by 2. Tell me B -- and tell me what B is NOT.
quick_checks.look_for: 'B = 10 square units; it's not 7 (that's adding the edges).' Hearing the contrast confirms the area meaning stuck.

quick_checks.prompt: Base area 6 sq cm, height 1/2 cm. Volume, in one line?
quick_checks.look_for: V = 6 x 1/2 = 3 cubic cm. A 6 1/2 diagnoses adding B and h; hunting for more numbers diagnoses not trusting B as an area.

worked_solution.stem: A prism's base is 4 cm by 3 cm, and its height is 2 1/2 cm. Use V = Bh to find its volume.

steps.annotation: B is the AREA of the base -- unit squares covering the bottom. Multiply the base edges, never add them.
The height counts how many base-layers stack up -- here, two and a half layers.
12 x 2 = 24, and half of 12 is 6. Add the pieces.
B wore square units; the volume wears CUBIC units.

faded_example.stem: A prism's base is 5 in. by 2 in., and its height is 1 1/2 in. Use V = Bh to find its volume.

steps.annotation: Find the base AREA first: multiply the base edges.
Set up V = B x h with your base area and the height.
Multiply and label in cubic units.

sentence_starters: B = ___ square units because the base is ___ times ___.
V = Bh worked because B already holds l x w -- then I multiplied by the height.

skills.name: Find a missing dimension or possible dimensions from a known volume
skills.i_do_script: Now we run the volume formula in reverse: the volume is known, and an edge is missing. Model with V = 15 cubic inches, length 3 in., width 2 1/2 in.: the two known edges give 3 x 2 1/2 = 7 1/2, and the missing height must satisfy 7 1/2 x h = 15, so h = 15 divided by 7 1/2 = 2 inches. Always finish with the forward check: 3 x 2 1/2 x 2 = 15. If a student multiplies everything in sight, the check exposes it immediately.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the volume by the known edges instead of dividing
canonical_error.example: V = 15 cubic inches, l = 3 in., w = 2 1/2 in.: student computes 15 x 3 x 2 1/2 = 112 1/2 instead of h = 15 / (3 x 2 1/2) = 2
canonical_error.why: Years of volume problems trained one reflex: multiply all the numbers. The student doesn't re-read the problem to notice the volume is now GIVEN and an edge is missing -- the formula must be undone with division, not run forward again.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- which number in this problem is the volume?
redirect_script.prompt: Circle the volume -- it's the ANSWER to l x w x h, not one of the edges. Write (known edge) x (known edge) x h = volume, multiply the two known edges, then divide the volume by that product to free h. Check by multiplying forward.
redirect_script.praise: You undid the formula with division and your forward check landed right on the volume. That's algebra thinking.

skills.item_template: The volume is given with two edges (or the base area), and the student finds the missing dimension; OR a cube count and unit-fraction edge are given, and the student finds the volume and proposes possible dimensions. NR or multi-part, spec Above Proficiency shape.

What is the height, h, of the prism, in centimeters?

A worker packs 64 cube-shaped boxes, each with side lengths of 1/4 ft, into a crate with no gaps. The crate is a rectangular prism.

Part A: What is the volume, in cubic feet, of the crate?

Part B: What are possible dimensions, in feet, of the crate?

vocabulary.definition: The unlabeled edge you solve for when the volume is already known.
A letter, like h, standing in for the number you're finding.
Operations that undo each other -- division undoes multiplication.
Any set of three edge lengths whose product equals the given volume.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.GM.3 -- volume and surface area of more complex solids.

worked_example_script.text: Display: 'A prism has a volume of 15 cubic inches. Its length is 3 in. and its width is 2 1/2 in. What is its height?' Show the figure with h = ? on the height edge.
Read carefully: which of these numbers is the VOLUME, and which are edges? How can you tell?
In past problems we multiplied three edges to GET the volume. What's different about what we know this time?
Write: 3 x 2 1/2 x h = 15.
What do the two known edges multiply to? So what times 7 1/2 equals 15?

If a student starts computing 15 x 3 x 2 1/2, stop the pencil: 'You just used 15 as an edge. Is 15 an edge or the finished volume?' Reread the stem together and re-sort the numbers before any arithmetic.
h = 15 / 7 1/2. How many 7 1/2s fit in 15?
h = 2 inches. Now the payoff habit -- check forward: 3 x 2 1/2 x 2 = 15. The check turns 'I think' into 'I know.'

practice_problems.stem: A prism's base area is 4 sq cm and its volume is 12 cubic cm. What is its height, in centimeters?
A prism has volume 8 cubic ft, length 4 ft, and width 2 ft. What is its height, in feet?
A prism has a volume of 9 cubic inches. Its length is 4 in. and its width is 1 1/2 in. What is its height, in inches?
practice_problems.notes: Watch for 54 (9 x 4 x 1 1/2) -- the multiply-everything reflex.

practice_problems.stem: A prism has a volume of 5 cubic cm. Its length is 2 1/2 cm and its width is 2 cm. What is its height, in centimeters?
A prism has a volume of 12 cubic feet, a length of 4 ft, and a width of 1 1/2 ft. Owen tried to find the height. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 2 ft. Owen multiplied the volume by the edges -- but 12 is the finished volume, not an edge. Undo the formula: 4 x 1 1/2 = 6, and h = 12 / 6 = 2. Check: 4 x 1 1/2 x 2 = 12. (A 72-ft-tall prism holding only 12 cubic feet makes no sense.)
practice_problems.notes: The multiply-everything error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: Exactly 40 cubes with 1/2-inch edges fill a box with no gaps. What is the volume of the box, in cubic inches?
A crate has a volume of 3 cubic feet, and every edge is a whole-number multiple of 1/2 ft. Give one possible set of dimensions for the crate.
practice_problems.answer: Answers vary. One possibility: 3 ft x 2 ft x 1/2 ft (3 x 2 x 1/2 = 3). Any three multiples of 1/2 whose product is 3 work.
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own -- spec Above shape, Part B.

practice_problems.stem: A prism's volume doubles, but its base area stays exactly the same. What happened to its height? Explain using V = Bh.
practice_problems.answer: The height doubled. In V = Bh, if B is unchanged and V doubles, h must double to keep the equation true -- height is the only factor left to carry the change.
practice_problems.notes: Reasoning about the formula's structure -- looking-forward thinking.

activities.title: Is 72 Feet Reasonable?
activities.instructions:
1. Show Owen's work (h = 12 x 4 x 1 1/2 = 72 ft) without comment.
2. First question to pairs: before checking any arithmetic, could a 72-foot-tall prism hold only 12 cubic feet? Why not?
3. Pairs sort the numbers (which is the volume? which are edges?), rewrite as 6 x h = 12, and solve.
4. Debrief: what reflex caused the error? (Multiply-everything.) What habit catches it? (Reasonableness + forward check.)

content.worked_problem: V = 12 cubic ft, l = 4 ft, w = 1 1/2 ft. Owen wrote: h = 12 x 4 x 1 1/2 = 72 ft.
content.error_step: Owen treated the given volume as another edge and multiplied everything together.
content.why: The volume is the RESULT of l x w x h. With V known, divide: 4 x 1 1/2 = 6, so h = 12 / 6 = 2 ft. The forward check 4 x 1 1/2 x 2 = 12 confirms it.

activities.title: Crate Designer
materials: A 'client order' card: 96 cube boxes, each with 1/4-ft edges
activities.instructions:
1. The client needs a crate that EXACTLY fits 96 cube boxes with 1/4-ft edges, no gaps.
2. Groups first find the crate's volume (96 x 1/64 = 1 1/2 cubic ft).
3. Each group designs TWO different crates (three dimensions each, every dimension a multiple of 1/4 ft) and verifies each design multiplies to 1 1/2.
4. Groups trade designs and check each other's with a forward multiplication.
5. Debrief: how many correct designs exist? Why more than one? (Volume fixes the product, not the shape.)

activities.title: Mystery Edge
activities.instructions:
1. Player A secretly picks three dimension cards, computes the volume, and reveals the volume plus TWO of the cards.
2. Player B finds the hidden edge and must say the division they used out loud.
3. Player A confirms by showing the hidden card; both check forward with l x w x h.
4. Swap roles. Score a point per correct recovery WITH a spoken forward check.

strategy_links.why: Studying a correct undo-the-formula solution next to the multiply-everything error is the fastest way to install the sorting step.
'Which number is the volume, and how do you know?' is the think-pair-share question this whole skill hinges on.
A think-aloud that sorts the givens (volume vs. edges) BEFORE computing models the self-questioning that prevents the reflex multiply.

questioning_prompts: Which number in this problem is the volume? Circle it before you touch your pencil.
What equation connects what you know to what's missing? Write it with the ? in place.
You divided -- by what, and why that number?
Check forward: multiply all three edges. Do you land on the given volume?
Is your answer reasonable -- could a prism with these edges really hold that volume?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies the given volume by the known edges -- e.g., h = 15 x 3 x 2 1/2 -- instead of dividing.
misconception_redirects.say: Circle the volume -- it's the ANSWER to l x w x h, not one of the edges. Write (known edge) x (known edge) x h = volume, multiply the two known edges, then divide the volume by that product to free h. Check by multiplying forward.
misconception_redirects.praise: You undid the formula with division and your forward check landed right on the volume. That's algebra thinking.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides the volume by only ONE known edge and stops -- e.g., h = 15 / 3 = 5.
misconception_redirects.say: Two edges are known, so combine them first: 3 x 2 1/2 = 7 1/2. THAT product is what h multiplies. Divide the volume by 7 1/2.
misconception_redirects.praise: You combined both known edges before dividing -- the missing edge came out clean, and the check proves it.

quick_checks.prompt: V = 10 cubic cm, l = 4 cm, w = 1/2 cm. Write ONLY the equation with h in it -- don't solve.
quick_checks.look_for: 4 x 1/2 x h = 10 (or h = 10 / 2). Anything starting '10 x 4' diagnoses the multiply-everything reflex.

quick_checks.prompt: You found h = 3. The edges were 2 and 1 1/2, volume 9. Prove your h in one line.
quick_checks.look_for: The forward check 2 x 1 1/2 x 3 = 9. Students who can't produce the check are guessing at the division.

worked_solution.stem: A prism has a volume of 15 cubic inches. Its length is 3 in. and its width is 2 1/2 in. What is its height?

steps.annotation: Sort the numbers first: 15 is the VOLUME (the product), 3 and 2 1/2 are edges, h is missing.
Combine the two known edges: 3 x 2 1/2 = 7 1/2.
Division undoes multiplication -- how many 7 1/2s make 15? Two.
Run the formula forward with your answer. Landing on 15 proves h = 2 in.

faded_example.stem: A prism has a volume of 6 cubic cm. Its length is 4 cm and its width is 1/2 cm. What is its height?

steps.annotation: Write the formula with the known edges and the missing h.
Combine the known edges first.
Divide the volume by that product to find h.
Check forward: multiply all three edges and confirm the volume.
